name: Rimbert
otherNames: Rimbertus, the form of the Latin Lives
Rembertus, a form in Mansi's headnotes
knownFor: Anskar's disciple, who followed him as archbishop of Hamburg and Bremen in 865 and, with a fellow disciple, wrote his Life, the main source for Anskar. The Life of Rimbert says he gave even the altar vessels, and once his own horse, to free captives.
dates: Chosen archbishop in 865, on the day of Anskar's burial, by the Life of Rimbert. Died 888, buried 11 June, by Adam of Bremen, who says he sat 23 years and took the years from a computus brought from Corbie. No source used here gives his year of birth
place: Turholt, in Flanders, where Anskar found him as a boy; Hamburg and Bremen, his see; New Corbey, where he took the monk's habit; Schleswig; Bremen, where he died and, Adam says, was buried outside Saint Peter's church on the east
role: Archbishop of Hamburg and Bremen; Anskar's biographer

keyWorks.title: Life of Anskar
keyWorks.about: written with a fellow disciple, the Life of Rimbert says, and addressed to the monks of Corbie. Georg Waitz says nearly all agree it was written at Hamburg before 876. It is used here in Waitz's Latin and C. H. Robinson's English

keyWorks.title: Letter to a woman vowed to God at Heresi and her sisters
keyWorks.about: held in Latin in the Life of Rimbert. Waitz's notes show that much of it is drawn from Gregory and Augustine

traces: C. H. Robinson says the Life of Anskar contains nearly all that is known of Anskar's life and work.
Waitz, quoting Dahlmann, says the Life of Anskar will always be counted among the foremost monuments of Germany.
The Life of Rimbert says he carried on Anskar's mission himself whenever other work allowed, kept priests in churches among the pagans across the sea, and was often shipwrecked.
remembered: The Life of Rimbert reports Anskar saying that Rimbert was worthier of an archbishop's office than he himself was of a subdeacon's.
Adam of Bremen compares Anskar and Rimbert to Elijah and Elisha.
The Life of Rimbert calls him the mildest of men, yet not to be moved from a judgment, for he said he took his guidance from visions of Anskar.

uncertain: His own life rests on one Life of Rimbert by an unnamed author. G. H. Pertz says it was written while Archbishop Adalgar lived, by a Bremen cleric or a monk of Corbie, who was not present at the death. The copy used here breaks off in its twenty-third chapter, before the death.
His death. The year 888 and the burial day, 11 June, come from Adam of Bremen, writing about 1073, from a computus brought from Corbie; Bernhard Schmeidler cites the Annals of Corvey for 888.
His birthplace. A note in Waitz's edition calls Turholt his birthplace; Robinson says only that Turholt was near it. The Life of Rimbert says only that Anskar found the boy and his parents there.

The priest Rimbert in the Life of Anskar. The Life says Anskar sent to Sweden a priest named Rimbert, of Danish descent. Dahlmann, in Waitz's edition, says this was a different man. Robinson says it is not clear, since Adam makes the author a deacon at this time, though Adam may have been mistaken.

The Frisian battle of 884. Adam, quoting Bovo of Corvey, says Christians encouraged by Rimbert defeated the Northmen, and that the Life of Rimbert leaves this out. Schmeidler says Bovo's lost work perhaps held miracle stories more than history.
His miracles. The Life of Rimbert says it is said he calmed storms and healed a blind man, and adds that it is not easily believed that any man of its own time did such things.
